title: Hellgates
author: Outpost
summary: How Hellgates work in the Dragonfire era: entry through the Antiquarian's Den, the IP floors and soft caps for 2v2 and 5v5, the healing debuff, the lava change in Dragonfire Patch 3, and the comps and fight habits that win lethal duos.

children: A Hellgate puts your party and one enemy party in the same demon-filled instance. You clear mobs, the lava starts rising, and at some point the two teams meet. The winners take the reward chest, and in lethal they also loot whatever the losers were wearing. Most small-scale players learn to fight in the 2v2: a mistake costs one set, and you come out of every loss knowing a bit more.
Older videos describe a different mode. Here's what has changed, oldest first:

Base loot and fame went up, loot no longer scales with Infamy, and the fame bonus from Infamy dropped from 50% to 20%. The winning team now heals and loses its debuffs after a victory, and the 2v2 Hell buff adds another 10% damage.

Build around the soft cap. A 1,300 IP player in a lethal gate fights at 1,170 (1,100 plus 35% of 200). A 1,000 IP player in a non-lethal gate fights at 910. Silver you spend past the cap buys you very little.
wear a cheap set that reaches 900 with your spec. Anything above that is wasted, and cheap gear is cheaper to repair.

Spec still matters below the cap.
Two players at the same item tier do not fight at the same IP if one has the weapon line levelled. Check your real number on the character sheet before you queue.
Enter the Den from the city, pick the mode and queue as a full party. The Den has a bank and a repair station, so gear up there.
You spawn on your side with demon packs between you and the other team. Clear them as you go. They give fame and loot, and fighting with a pack on your back loses fights.
The lava rises over time and pushes both teams into a smaller space. Rising Lava stacks stay on you after a knockdown, and molten lava breaks shields.
The run gets decided when the teams meet. A knocked-down player stays down for up to 10 minutes, so a 2v1 is usually over.
The winners heal up, get their debuffs cleansed and open the reward chest. In lethal, the losers' gear is lying on the ground too.

Kills in Hellgates can drop a Hell Memento kill trophy, and every win builds Antiquarian Standing for the Den's mounts and cosmetics. Hellgates also count toward the Conqueror's Challenge under one merged Hellgates category since Season 31.

Most duos that work are a healer plus a damage dealer, or two bruisers who can look after themselves. With a 35% healing debuff a healer can't out-heal focused burst on their own, so the healer also has to bring crowd control or peel.
Holy and Nature Staffs are the common start. See the

Since Radiant Wilds the in-game Armory ranks builds by win rate for each activity and group size, using real match data. Look there to see what's winning this month and adapt from it.

In 5v5 you want a frontline that can start the fight and a backline that hits the same target. Bring one healer. The extra Healing Sickness on two-healer teams exists to stop double-healer stall. Rotcaller Staff's Plaguebringer is the strongest anti-heal in 5v5, and Dragonfire Patch 3 raised its cooldown from 30s to 35s, so count that window when you play against it.
Since Dragonfire Patch 3 anyone standing in lava takes far more damage from players. Zone the enemy into it and don't kite through it yourself.
Pick one target and stay on it.
Two players splitting damage lose to two players who focus.
Kill or lock the healer first
when you can reach them. Most duos fall apart as soon as their healer is under pressure.
Save your defensive for their burst
if you play melee. Open ground favours kiting ranged builds.
Clear the packs before you engage.
A good duo with demons on it will lose to an average one.

Healing Potions heal a share of your health that scales with IP, and Dragonfire Patch 4 lowered that share at every tier (900 IP: 18% to 16%; 1,100 IP: 22% to 19.5%). Expect less from your potions than older guides do.

Start in non-lethal. You learn the same things, and a loss only costs repairs. Move up to lethal once you're winning more than you lose in non-lethal and can afford to replace your set three or four times. For a week, write down what each set costs and what each run brings home. Price your sets in the

children: The Mists are short-lived instanced zones for solo players and duos. You follow a wisp in the open world, step through its portal, and farm camps, chests and resources while other small parties do the same. The mode was quiet for a long time until Radiant Wilds Patch 3 (June 2026) rebuilt the rewards, and now it's a good solo farm again. It's also how you get to Brecilien.

children: Your first silver comes from boring, repeatable work in safe zones. Pick one method below and stick with it for a few evenings, and you'll have enough for a proper set, a transport mount and some money in reserve. Ignore the "fastest silver" videos that send day-one characters into red zones. Those routes only pay if you can afford to lose a set every hour.
Since the Abyssal Depths update (June 2025) a new character picks a starting path in the Albion Journal's First Steps category:

children: Levelling a gathering line is a fame race, and you get there faster by hitting lots of cheap nodes quickly than a few rare ones slowly. Most players who feel stuck at T6 spend their evenings riding from one T7 node to the next. Gather the plentiful lower tiers in the matching gear and you'll unlock things much sooner.
There are five lines: wood, ore, fiber, hide and stone. Each one levels separately, and gathering gear only helps its own resource. If you split your time early, you level two lines at half speed.

children: The Roads of Avalon are a maze of full-loot zones connected by temporary portals. Every portal has a player limit and a timer, so tonight's network won't be there tomorrow. Small groups go in for chests, high-tier resources, tracking and fights, and use the Roads as a shortcut across the map. Those portal limits are why small groups like it here: a forty-player zerg can't follow a seven-player group through a seven-player portal.
Avalonian portals open in the open world and take you into a Road. Inside, more portals connect Roads to each other and lead back out.

The Royal Continent has the blue, yellow and red zones around the Royal Cities, and the Outlands are all black. Orange rules only apply in instances: the Depths, and the Ancient Lands when you open them from a yellow zone.

Since Dragonfire, if you've been knocked down for more than 30 seconds in a blue or yellow zone, you can respawn at the nearest region entrance. That doesn't apply to outlaws, players in faction combat, or anyone inside an open-PvP subzone.
Practise PvP in yellow zones, where it only costs you repairs.

You respawn with nothing at your home or the last city you visited. Red zones are the first real risk a gatherer or hauler meets on the Royal Continent, and every road into Caerleon goes through them.

toc.title: Where runes, souls and relics come from

children: Enchanting raises an item's enchantment level at the Artifact Foundry. Each level adds roughly one tier's worth of Item Power, so a T6.1 sword sits level with a T7.0. The real question is cost: are the runes, souls or relics cheaper than just buying the enchanted item? On a busy market they often aren't.
You can't skip a step, so taking a .0 item to .3 eats runes, then souls, then relics. The material has to match the item's tier (T6 runes for a T6 item), from
at T4 up to Elder's at T8.

The count doesn't change between steps or tiers. Only the slot matters:

Taking a two-handed weapon from .0 to .3 costs 384 runes, 384 souls and 384 relics of its tier. So two-handed weapons are where buying enchanted is most often cheaper, and helmets and boots are where enchanting most often pays.
Food and potions don't use runes. Enchanted meals take Fish Sauce and enchanted potions take Arcane Extract, and the amount depends on the item.
in any city. Drop the item in, check what materials it wants and confirm.
Runes, souls and relics never come back, so city bonuses, focus and return rate do nothing. Enchant wherever your bank is.
Excellent and Masterpiece items keep their quality when enchanted, which can make a good .0 roll worth upgrading.

In this case buying the .1 is 14,400 cheaper, and that's before the order fees on the runes. On a helmet the same rune price only adds 33,600, and the answer often flips. Do the sums item by item, in the city where you'll actually buy or sell.

Since each enchantment level adds about a tier of Item Power, a T4.3, T5.2, T6.1 and T7.0 of the same item end up close in IP. Price every equivalent version before you enchant anything. Depending on the week, the cheapest way to a target IP might be a lower tier at a higher enchantment, or the reverse.
Higher-tier items cost more to repair, which adds up in content where you get knocked down a lot.
Where content has an IP soft cap, like yellow zones at 1,200 or lethal Hellgates at 1,100, the cheapest item that hits the cap wins.

takes the item, the step and your prices. It counts the runes, souls or relics from the game's upgrade data, prices them from the market and tells you whether upgrading beats buying the enchanted item. If a price is missing it shows as unavailable, never as zero.

They drop from most PvE and PvP content, open world and dungeons through to Hellgates, and higher-tier zones drop higher-tier ones. You can also buy them on the market at every tier. People who farm dungeons and the Mists often sit on stacks they never touch. If you've got some in the bank, spend them on your own gear before buying more.
Enchanting a two-handed weapon without pricing the enchanted version first.
Using the wrong tier of rune. The foundry only takes the item's own tier.

title: Your first ZvZ
author: Outpost
summary: What you need for your first guild ZvZ in Season 34 and later: how a zerg splits into parties, what each role does, the calls you'll hear, how Disarray and the battle mount limit work, the Resilience Penetration test, Lifeward Potions, regear rules and the mistakes callers spot first.

toc.title: What callers notice in new players

children: ZvZ (zerg versus zerg) is Albion's big guild PvP, with dozens of players a side fighting over territories, castles, outposts, Fortresses and Dragon Attacks. Your first one will be chaos: thirty voices, a caller shouting abilities, and a fight that's done in forty seconds. You don't have to follow all of it. Get in the right party, wear the right gear and do what your party lead tells you.
A zerg is split into parties, each with its own job:
tanks, usually with the caller. They start the fight.
keep the frontline alive and cleanse it.
purges, shields, damage buffs and crowd control.
follow the engage and hit what it catches. Many guilds run a
that dives in for one big burst of area damage.
experienced players ride these to disrupt or engage.
Your officer puts you in a party, and you stay there. Swapping because a friend is in another party wrecks the plan.
Ask for the approved build list.
Most ZvZ guilds keep one per role, with a required IP. The builds are picked to work together, so a good build that's off the list is still the wrong build.
and set push-to-talk. Most callers want quiet during fights.
A lot of guilds replace a set you lose in an official fight, as long as you wore an approved build and followed calls. Some want a screenshot or a death recap.

Since Dragonfire the Loadouts window has an "All" column that sets quality and enchantment for every slot in one go, and since Dragonfire Patch 2 you can share loadouts as text. Ask your officer for the guild's loadout string.
that go with the build, and keep a spare set in the bank.
Builds people often start on, from the library:

For Season 34 the developers set Resilience Penetration to zero on every weapon and spell as a test, to move the meta away from Plate melee damage. Claymore, Dual Swords, daggers, axes and the rest all lost it. Check the Season 35 patch notes to see if it comes back.

, which uses Dragon Blood. It shields nearby allies from one fatal blow and revives them the first time they'd die. Dragonfire Patch 4 raised its range from 11m to 14m so ranged supports can use it. If your guild hands them out, save yours for when the enemy bomb lands.
Dragonfire Patch 4 cut them at every tier, and more at high IP (1,200 IP: 24% to 21%).

Intimidating Aura went from a 70% to a 40% damage decrease in Dragonfire.
Big groups in the open world get

Ancient Ent, Battle Rhino, Phalanx Beetle, Siege Ballista

When in doubt, follow the people in your party.

Running ahead of the caller and dying alone.

title: Your first PvE build
author: Outpost
summary: Picking a first solo PvE build that clears packs, heals itself and gets away, why sticking to one weapon line beats spreading across three, what the 1,200 IP soft cap and the Dragonfire mob changes mean for your gear, and how to find, price and save a tested loadout on Outpost.
dek: Picking a first solo PvE build that clears packs, heals itself and gets away.

toc.title: The three tests every solo build must pass
Choose a weapon line and stay on it
What the current rules mean for your gear
Find a tested loadout on Outpost
Save your version and take it out

children: Your first solo set has three jobs. It has to kill packs of three to six mobs without stopping to rest, keep you alive with no healer, and be cheap enough that dying costs you an evening of farming at most. The rest of this guide is about doing that on a budget, in content that pays for it.
The three tests every solo build must pass
Check any build you find against these before you buy a single piece.

Most open-world camps, solo dungeon rooms and Corrupted Dungeon corridors are packs. A single-target weapon handles bosses fine and everything else slowly, and slow clears are where solo players lose silver per hour.
Lifesteal, a self-heal, a shield or a strong defensive cooldown. Without one you're eating after every second pull.
A dash, a speed burst or a purge. In a yellow zone it gets you out of a bad pull. In the Mists or a Corrupted Dungeon it gets you away from another player.
Not many weapons tick all three, so let the armor cover the gap. A weapon with no sustain wants a healing chest or helmet; one with no mobility wants boots with a dash or speed.
Choose a weapon line and stay on it
decides how strong a piece is. Tier, enchantment and quality raise it, and so does
on the Destiny Board. Levels in one weapon's specialist node add IP to that weapon, and its mastery levels add IP to every weapon in the line.

So switching lines hurts. Someone with a month in Fire Staff hits far harder with a Fire Staff than with a Sword they picked up yesterday at the same tier. Pick a line you like, give it a few weeks, and put your fame and Learning Points there. Since the Abyssal Depths update, Learning Points work through
: fame on a node with Quick Learn on gets multiplied by five while the points drain. Turn it on for the one node you care about and leave the rest of the board alone. The
keeps a record of your levels.
Big area damage and plenty of tested rotations. Dragonfire raised the Hoarfrost Staff's Avalanche damage and halved its knockback against mobs to help solo clears.
Cloth armor and no self-heal, so the armor has to supply sustain.
Sturdy melee lines, cheap at low tiers, with good sustain options.
Dragonfire made the axe Adrenaline Boost expire if you stop hitting an enemy for 3 seconds.
Range keeps you out of most mob mechanics.
You have to kite, and bow players usually die kiting into a second pack.
You kill slowly, but you're very hard to kill.
Clear speed. Fine while you learn, poor for silver per hour later on.
The Bloodmoon Staff is the library's most liked solo farming build.
Radiant Wilds Patch 2 halved Tear Open's Blood Pool heal (61 to 30), so it relies more on armor sustain now.
The popular solo builds shift with each balance patch. See what people are running this month before you trust a video from two seasons back. The in-game
is useful for this. Since Radiant Wilds it ranks builds by real gameplay data, and since Dragonfire it shows damage, healing, kills and deaths per hour along with each build's average IP.
What the current rules mean for your gear
Three changes from the past year decide how much you should spend on gear.

Since Abyssal Depths, blue and yellow open-world zones, their static dungeons, yellow Mists and the Knightfall Abbeys that mirror them soft-cap Item Power at 1,200 and keep only 20% of anything over it. Randomized dungeons ignore the cap. Paying for 1,400 IP to farm a yellow zone throws away most of the extra silver.

Dragonfire cut the most damage reduction you can stack on a mob from 80% to 50%, and the health reduction from 50% to 25%. Single abilities dropped too: Guardian Armor's Enfeeble Aura went from 60% to 25% against mobs, Mercenary Hood's Howl from 30% to 20%. Builds that relied on debuffing mobs until they were harmless need real sustain now.

Knockdown in yellow zones lasts 90 seconds. After 30 seconds knocked down in a blue or yellow open-world region you can respawn at the nearest region entrance, unless you're an outlaw, in Faction Warfare combat or in an open-PvP area. Durability loss and repair costs also go down when a cap lowers your item's power.
Find a tested loadout on Outpost
Filter to a weapon you've specced or plan to spec.
Read the description for the content it was made for, the IP the author aimed at and the rotation.
Check every slot against your budget. A set full of artifact pieces is useless if you can't replace it twice.

Food is the long buff and the potion is your panic button. Most solo builds list both. A

is the normal starter potion. Dragonfire Patch 4 (2 November 2026) cut Healing Potion healing at every IP level, and more at the top: 16% to 14% at 800 IP, 24% to 21% at 1,200 IP. If a build was tuned around the old potion, you'll probably want one more piece of sustain. Buy enough for the whole session before you leave town, since riding back for one potion costs more than the potion. Eat before the first pull rather than after the first bad one.
Prices change by city and by day. Open your build and use

to price every slot at the build's quality in whichever city you pick, for one set or several. A slot with no sell order stays unpriced rather than counting as free, so you can see what's still missing. The
shows each city's orders for a single piece, with when each price was seen.
Buy one set to wear and keep the silver for a second. If a death leaves you with nothing to wear, you lose a day of farming. The spare set means you can play without worrying about it.

title: Corrupted Dungeons
author: Outpost
summary: Farming Corrupted Dungeons for chests and fame while dodging the PvP: entry IP for Hunter, Stalker and Slayer, the four-chest route, boss bar point counts, breaking Demonic Shards to banish an invader, and the patch changes behind the mode in Season 34.

toc.title: Changes that shape the mode now

children: A Corrupted Dungeon is a solo instance where the game can match another player in to hunt you. "Ratting" means going in for the mobs and chests and banishing the invader when one shows up, instead of fighting. Done well it's one of the steadiest solo silver farms in the game, and most of your runs end without you trading a single hit.
You can go in from the Antiquarian's Den in any royal city or from open-world entrances. Since Abyssal Depths the entry check uses your
Item Power. Food and spec bonuses don't count toward it.

is your Corrupted rating. It unlocks Slayer and gives up to 20% extra fame, but since Abyssal Depths it doesn't make chests any richer. Base loot and fame went up at the same time to compensate, so a fresh character's chests match a veteran's at the same difficulty. Both lethal tiers soft-cap Item Power, so the last hundred IP on a set costs far more than it gives you. Check the cap in the entrance panel before you pay for it.
Changes that shape the mode now

entry from the Antiquarian's Den, faster matchmaking, PvP in Corrupted Dungeons counting toward Antiquarian Standing, map items salvaging for 100% of their value, and a heal and debuff wipe after you win.
Book Chests and Hidden Treasures are gone. Every treasure spawn is a Treasure Chest now.
no trading inside, and Hunter bosses and minibosses hit softer.
the Corrupted Dungeon healing debuff went from 30% to 40%. Self-heal builds took a bigger hit than burst builds.
lower mob debuff caps (most damage reduction on a mob 80% to 50%), so builds that relied on debuffing bosses need more sustain of their own.
A rat build wants quick pack damage and at least two ways to make distance. Three tested setups:
Druid Robe for burst, plus Shoes of Tenacity. Radiant Wilds Patch 2 made its Tornado about 10% faster.
with the same robe. Razor Cut does damage and moves you.

The library lists them at T8 for reference. In Stalker, a specced weapon at about T7-equivalent IP keeps the pace up. In Slayer, aim for around 1,400 to 1,500 displayed IP and stop there. Buy T4 or T6 Poison Potions for clears, since T8 is wasted on a farming loop. Eat Avalonian Beef Stew, and move up to
the .1 version in Slayer if your margin allows. More current Corrupted setups are in

Every layout has two minibosses with a chest each, a treasure chest guarded by mobs and the final boss chest. Open all four on every run. You make more per hour from chests than from clearing everything.
Read the map before moving. Mark both minibosses, the treasure room and the boss room.
Kill the closest miniboss and open its chest. Pick up compact packs on the way and skip lone mobs in dead ends.
Clear the guarded treasure room if it's on your way.
Before the second miniboss, get the boss bar to
Kill the second miniboss. Its 100 (Stalker) or 400 (Slayer) points fill the bar, spawn the final boss and
Kill the boss, open chest four and go straight into the next dungeon.

Five to six minutes a run is a good pace you can keep up, which means one food buff covers five or six runs. If you're averaging ten minutes, sort out the route or the build before spending on Slayer gear.
Normal mobs come in three weights, and Slayer values are four times the Stalker ones.
Mage, Arbalist, Slaver, Mauler, Thief, Predator
The two minibosses give 200 of 500 in Stalker and 800 of 2,000 in Slayer, so normal mobs have to make up the other 300 or 1,200. Count in units (low 1, medium 3, high 5) and you need

in either tier. Imps are cheap progress for their health and Mages make good medium targets; long detours for one Predator rarely pay off. Go by the live bar rather than your count, because it already includes what you killed along the way.
Don't touch the invasion shrine. All it does is sign you up to invade other people. You can be invaded right up until the final boss spawns. When the warning comes up:
Stop the route, and don't drag a pack along behind you.
and, on Druid Robe builds, the robe to
. Do it early and out of combat, and let the ability-change cooldown run out.
on the minimap. Taking an outer loop usually keeps you clear of the invader.
Break one, move straight away, break the next. Three shards banish the invader.
Put your PvE skills back before the next pull.
Force Field knocks a chaser off you, and Frost Shield covers you while you hit a shard. Your weapon's movement skills are part of the escape, so stop using them on mobs once the warning shows. A
thrown into a corridor the invader has to come through buys you several seconds.
Once you start the banish, finish it. Breaking two shards and then turning to fight leaves you with neither plan working.
five to ten runs teach you the boss attacks, the route and the shard run. If you're experienced you can skip it.
farm full runs until your Infamy hits 100,000. Note your rating before and after a few runs to get your average.
move up once your gear, pace and banish plan are reliable. Go back to Stalker if lost sets are eating the profit.
Runs left to Slayer = (100,000 − current Infamy) ÷ your average net Infamy per run, rounded up.
After every boss chest, decide whether to:
if the food's still up, the loot is nothing special and you've still got the consumables an invasion needs.
if one drop, or the whole bag, is worth more than you're willing to lose.
if you're out of food or potions, or the last invasion exposed a hole in the build.
Judge the method over twenty runs, not one jackpot or one death. Log banked loot, time, consumables and lost sets, and work out silver per hour. Price a replacement set in the
before you go in, and save your final loadout with

title: Black zone gathering
author: Outpost
summary: Gathering in the Outlands and keeping most of what you pick up: a set you can afford to lose, mount carry weights from game data, basing out of a Smuggler's Den, the patch changes gatherers should know, spotting a scout early, and an escape to drill until you don't have to think about it.

toc.title: Decide three numbers at the bank

children: Albion's best nodes, high tier and high enchantment, are in the black zones of the Outlands, and so are the players who hunt gatherers. Anyone out there can kill you and take everything you're wearing and carrying. You will lose sets. What you're aiming for is losing them rarely and cheaply, and banking often enough that the good trips cover the bad ones.
Decide three numbers at the bank
Bring a set and mount you could replace ten times over. If losing it would make you play scared, drop a tier.
How much you're carrying before you turn round and bank. Pick a number you'd hate to lose, scaled to your own bankroll.
Thirty minutes, an hour, longer. It decides your mount and how much food to pack.
Write them down. Nearly every bad gathering death starts with "one more node" after the threshold.
Your set needs to raise yield on the resource you came for and buy you enough time to remount after a dismount.
The gathering cap and garb for that resource, for yield. Since Rogue Frontier Patch 2 every gathering cap has
, which strips lingering damage over time so a DoT tick doesn't break your Invisibility Potion or remount.
and the other gatherer boots are fine, and so is a combat pair with a dash.
A weapon with movement or a defensive cooldown.
An escape cape such as a
, which chains Iron Will, Ambush and Flee into one escape. Dragonfire Patch 2 also made Spinning Blades immune to transformation effects while you're in the air. There's more in
Tools for every resource you plan to gather. Since Abyssal Depths Patch 2 you
cannot swap gathering tools in combat
, so if a tool breaks or you forgot one mid-fight, you're stuck without it.
. Since Rogue Frontier Patch 5 their damage reduction lasts while you're invisible and for 2 seconds after you're revealed.
for every half hour you plan to be out, plus a spare.
if you'll be working high-enchant nodes, where the yield bonus pays for the potion.
Empty gathering journals for the tier you'll gather.
These are each mount's carry weight bonus at normal quality, taken from game data, before your own load and bag. Higher quality adds a bit.
Short, valuable trips near an exit

Capacity is only useful if you fill it, and a big mounted capacity becomes a trap once the mount dies and you're overweight on foot. The Gallant Horse's charge and the Direboar's invisibility both put your boots on cooldown, so only use them when the escape is worth it right then. Realm Divided raised Salamander mount carry weight, so they're now a real option for gathering. Mount prices change, so check them in the
; every mount's speed and carry weight is in the
Rogue Frontier moved Outlands banking into
. There are 35, each with two entrances in the same region, and each has a bank, a repair station, an Artifact Foundry, a Travel Planner and a Smuggler's Market.
Outlaws and players in combat cannot enter.
That makes a den the nearest thing to a safe door in the black zone, and you can ride in and mount up inside.
for +2.5% combat and gathering fame in the Outlands, and so you can travel back to it (without luggage only).

joins every den and Outlands Rest market into one order book. You can buy from a far-off den for a distance fee paid by whoever completes the trade, with no Premium discount. The market has a distance column and a Max Distance filter, and prices include the fee by default.
Everyone shares the den, gankers too. Watch the exit before you ride out with a full bag.

Guild territories and hideouts also work as bases, with closer exits and friends around, but your guildmates are after the same nodes. A portal town is fine for a planned trip to one biome if you don't mind longer rides.
Level one line to T8 first.
Wear that resource's gear and gather the plentiful T4 to T6 nodes. Steady common nodes level you faster than the rare T7 and T8 spawns.
once your lines are high: roam T6 to T8 zones, go after enchanted nodes and bring every tool you've levelled.
Habits that pay off on a route:
Check the middle of each map. Most gatherers stick to the edges, so central nodes get less traffic.
Don't wait at an empty T7 or T8 node. Respawn times vary too much for camping to be worth it.

show up in T5 to T8 regions and last a whole day. Some have Verdant Wisps that open a Resource Mist. Small ones are solo, Medium ones can have other players in them, and since Abyssal Depths a Legendary Resource Mist is always T8.
moved in Dragonfire. They spawn in T6+ Outlands regions that have their resource, with no announcement and no map marker.
are less aggressive since Dragonfire, and since Rogue Frontier their T4, T6 and T8 versions spawn fully charged, same as the odd tiers.
Check the region's player count on the map. The Outlands show 16 to 30 and 31 to 50 as separate ranges, and if there's a crowd you can't explain, leave.

A scout keeps an eye on you while their friends move in off-screen. Treat someone as a scout if they copy two of your direction changes, ride alongside you instead of passing, sit between you and an exit, or ride ahead and come back. You don't need proof to leave.
so nameplates don't get lost behind the interface.
anyone you don't know. Gank builds tend to use maces, claws, bear paws, Graveguard and Knight armor, and Sticky Potions.
If a player on foot with no mount health bar is near you, turn away now.
Keep game sound on. You can hear a dismount or an Invisibility Potion close by.

Portals spawn in the open world, and since Patch 1 they show on the World Map from any distance. A new portal stays locked for a while, then opens for a short entry window.

toc.title: Pick items that trade every day

children: Flipping makes silver off the market itself. You post a buy order below what the item sells for, wait for someone to fill it, then list it higher. You never leave town. What kills flips is arithmetic: forget one fee and the 8% profit you thought you had turns into a loss.

The order window shows the exact silver before you confirm, so compare it with this table once on your server. You don't get setup fees back when you cancel or an order expires. A buy order locks up its silver the moment you post it, so in practice your limit is how much silver you can afford to have sitting in orders.

A seller fills it and the item lands in your market box.
It sells. With Premium the game keeps 4% tax (11,600); without, 8% (23,200).

Spread here means the gap between your buy and sell price, as a share of what you paid. Under these numbers you lose money before the price even moves:

Each figure is (1 + buy fee) ÷ (1 − tax − sell fee) − 1. The last row is the standard order-to-order flip, and even with Premium it needs close to a 10% gap. Each relist costs another 2.5% of the listing, so if you expect to change the price twice, you need 5% more room.
Pick items that trade every day
A wide gap on something that sells twice a week is a bad flip. You end up holding stock while the price drifts. What to look for:
The in-game sales history shows what people paid and how many sold. Ten sales a day is worth more than one big sale a week.
The item details window shows an estimated market value, per item and (since Radiant Wilds) for the stack. Bid under it, sell near it.
A gap bigger than your break-even.
If the top buy order and the lowest sell order are closer than the table above, move on.
You'll notice a bad price on gear you wear long before you notice one on a recipe you've never crafted.

If another flipper tops your buy order by one silver and you answer with one silver, you're in a bidding war and both of you pay the setup fee every round. Jump 5 to 10% in one go instead. You're then first in line for the next seller, and plenty of flippers give up on an item once someone shows they'll pay more. When things go quiet, cancel and repost lower so you keep buying cheap. Each repost costs 2.5% of the order, so count it.
When selling, list just under the cheapest offer. Round-looking prices read cheaper in a list: 7,989,000 looks lower than 8,021,938, and 999 looks lower than 1,000 for one silver of difference.
Undercut by a little. Going 10% under the market to sell faster just gives your profit to the buyer, and it drags the price down for everyone, your next batch included.
Spread your silver over several items so one slow seller doesn't lock up your whole bankroll.
Keep a list of your open orders and their prices. The market box fills up while you're offline.
Recheck before you relist. If the price has dropped under your cost, either wait or take the small loss early.
Start by flipping in one city. Cross-city trades put you on the road;
Buy orders work for your own crafting too. If you never buy materials instantly, you save the spread on every one of them.

You buy in city A, carry it to city B and sell. What you keep is:

Check a recipe in five steps

children: Every craft and refine gives you back part of the materials you put in. That share is the

and converts it to a return rate once:
A bonus of 18 gives 18 ÷ 118 = 15.25%. Bonuses are added first and the formula runs once, so a city bonus plus focus gives you less than the two rates added together.
In a royal city the bonus is made of:
when you refine that city's resource.
when you craft one of the city's specialty item groups.

To get a real cost, multiply your materials by (1 − RRR). Refining T6 bars in Thetford with focus uses about 46% of the ore the recipe suggests. Islands, hideouts and other stations outside the royal cities have their own values, so read the station's rate in game before planning around one. The calculators'

What returns and what never does
Raw and refined resources come back.
Artifacts, faction tokens and enchanting materials (runes, souls, relics) never do

Same with the faction-heart refining recipes. You can make a T6 bar from three Runite Ore, a T5 bar and a Mountainheart instead of four ore and a bar, but the heart never comes back, so your rate only applies to the ore and bar. Outpost's
calculators leave non-returnable inputs out of the return no matter what you tick.

Each recipe has a base focus cost. In Outpost's recipe data that's 54 for a T4 bar, 94 for T5, 164 for T6, 287 for T7 and 503 for T8.

For refining, each level in any tier of a resource's refining line (Master Ore Smelter, say) adds 30 efficiency to every tier of that resource, and each level in the tier you're refining adds 250 more. With only Master Ore Smelter at 100 you have 28,000 efficiency for T6 bars, so a T6 bar costs 164 ÷ 2^2.8 ≈ 23.5 focus and a day's 10,000 focus covers about 425 bars. All five tiers at 100 gets you 40,000 on each tier, which is a sixteenth of the base cost.
Crafting works the same way with different weights. A specialist node gives most of its efficiency to its own item and a smaller share to its siblings. Dragonfire changed two of those sibling shares:
15 to 12.5 efficiency per sibling level, and quality bonus 0.375 to 0.3125, to make room for the Dragonslayer set.

Heal, Energy, Gigantify, Resistance, Sticky, Poison and Invisibility Brewer and the Bootlegger now give 22.5 per sibling level (from 18); Calming, Cleansing, Acid, Berserk, Hellfire, Gathering, Tornado and the new Lifeward Brewer give 11.25.
Once you max one item, focus-crafting it is far cheaper than anything next to it. So serious crafters pick a few items and stick with them. Enter your levels once in

Higher tiers cost a lot more focus per craft. A T8 refine can earn more per item than T5 and still earn less per focus.
Keep an eye on the daily bonuses. Holding focus for a +20 day in your refining city gets you about four extra points of return over a normal day.

title: Reading market prices
author: Outpost
summary: What the lowest sell order and the highest buy order tell you, why server, tier, enchantment, quality, city and the age of a price count as much as the number itself, where Outpost's prices come from, and why an unavailable price is never zero.
dek: What the lowest sell order and the highest buy order tell you, and what counts as much as the number.

toc.title: The two sides of the book
Match the item before you compare
Check how old the price is

children: Every item in every city has two prices: what sellers are asking and what buyers are offering. Most bad trades come from reading the wrong one, comparing two items that aren't the same, or trusting a price that was right yesterday. The
shows both sides for one item in every city, each with the time someone saw it.
The two sides of the book
is the cheapest price any seller is asking. If you buy instantly, this is what you pay.
is the best price any buyer is offering. If you sell instantly, this is what you get.
The gap between them is the

. The Market Explorer shows it as sell minus buy, as a share of the buy price. Trading instantly gives up the spread in exchange for speed. Orders keep it, but cost you time and a 2.5% setup fee each, and every sale pays 4% tax with Premium or 8% without. An order-to-order flip needs about a 9.6% spread with Premium just to break even; the
Match the item before you compare
Two prices are only comparable when everything else matches:
Europe, Americas and Asia are separate economies. Outpost's region switch changes every price on the page.
A T6.1 sword and a T6 sword are different items with separate books. In item IDs the enchantment comes after an @, so T6_MAIN_SWORD is the flat Broadsword and T6_MAIN_SWORD@1 is the 6.1.
Normal, Good, Outstanding, Excellent and Masterpiece all trade separately. A Masterpiece listing tells you nothing about the Normal price.

Each royal city, Brecilien and Caerleon has its own books, and the Black Market in Caerleon is a buyer of its own. The Outlands' Smuggler's Network is another separate market, linked across every den.

Outpost keeps each price with its own city, quality and side of the book. It won't blend a Lymhurst sell order and a Martlock buy order into one figure. If the quality you asked for has no data, you see the other qualities next to it, each with its own city and time, and none of them is passed off as the one you wanted.
Check how old the price is
A price is a snapshot from the moment someone saw it. A sell order seen ten minutes ago is a fair guide. One from two days ago may have filled, been cancelled or been undercut since.
In the Market Explorer each price shows its age, with the exact UTC time on hover. Anything older than an hour gets a

chip, and the city table's header counts how many orders are older than an hour. Buy and sell sides have separate times, so you can see a fresh sell order next to a stale buy order for the same item in the same city. If the cheaper city's price is a lot older, the comparison is a guess. Confirm it in game before you ride across the map.
to see how the average moved over the last 7 or 30 days. In a quiet market a single spike is often just one sale.
If nobody has uploaded a price for an item in a city, Outpost shows a dash and

. That means there's no data. The item isn't free, and the market isn't necessarily empty. A price observed as 0 gets the same treatment. If any input is missing, the calculators keep the result unavailable so a gap can't turn into a fake profit, and any price you type yourself is labelled as yours.

using a client that reads the market windows they open. Busy items in busy cities update often. Rare items, quiet cities and the Asia server can go a long time between uploads, and gaps in exact-quality T8 prices are common. The data is crowd-sourced and there's no guarantee on it.

A listing doesn't prove stock or volume. The order might be for one item, or someone else might grab it first. For anything expensive, open the market in game and check the order before spending silver. Since Radiant Wilds the game's item details window has shown an estimated market value per item and per stack, which is handy as a second opinion.

The Black Market in Caerleon buys equipment and hands it out as loot from mobs and chests all over the world. It only buys, so in Outpost its price is a buy order you can sell into and never something you can buy at. Selling there pays sales tax but no setup fee, since the sale is instant. Its demand follows what players loot and lose, so a high Black Market price on a niche item can disappear after a few sales. Check its time like any other price, and compare it with the Caerleon market's own buy orders before you craft for it.

title: Real profit
author: Outpost
summary: How to cost a trade or a craft so the profit still holds in game: purchase price, setup fees, sales tax with and without Premium, the trip between cities, margin versus return on investment, station fees and which returned materials to count. Worked examples included, and you can repeat them in Outpost.

toc.title: Crafting and refining: returns and two kinds of profit
Your typed prices stay marked as yours

children: Sell price minus buy price is the first number everyone looks at, and it's always too high. A trade only makes money once every fee, tax and trip is counted. Outpost's calculators put each cost on its own line so you don't miss one. Here's what goes on each line.
per item, and whether you buy instantly from a sell order or post a buy order.
per item, and whether you sell instantly into a buy order or list a sell order.
, and whether the market will take that many at that price.
What it costs to move them
, if the buy and sell cities differ.
Instant buy from a sell order
Instant sale to the Black Market

Selling instantly into a buy order skips the sell setup fee but you still pay tax. The game keeps setup fees when you cancel, so every relist pays again. Outpost doesn't assume your rates: the trade check, transport and production tools start tax and setup at 0, so type 4 and 2.5 (or 8 and 2.5 without Premium) yourself. The route scanner on the flipping page is the one exception and starts at 4 and 2.5.
Say you buy 10 items with a buy order at 10,000 each and sell them on sell orders at 12,000, with Premium.
The raw gap was 20,000 and fees ate more than half of it. Without Premium the tax is 9,600 and profit drops to 4,900. In
, enter the two prices and the quantity, set the purchase order fee, sales tax and sell order setup fee, and you get the same 9,700 plus the
Outpost shows both, and they divide by different things:
= profit ÷ what you sold for. Here 9,700 ÷ 120,000 = 8.1%.

Return tells you where to put limited silver: a 9.5% flip that turns over in a day is better than a 20% flip that sits for a week. Margin tells you how much room you have if the price drops before you sell. Thin margin on a volatile item is how most trades end up as losses.

Buying in one city and selling in another adds the trip: mount upkeep, repairs, any travel cost and a risk allowance for what you might lose. The risk allowance is the chance of losing a load times its value. A 2,000,000 silver load on a red-zone road where you lose one run in ten carries 200,000 of expected loss per run, and it goes in the sum. The
splits a load into trips by weight and adds the cost per trip plus whatever risk you set.
explains how to choose that number.
Crafting and refining: returns and two kinds of profit
Crafting and refining give back part of your materials. That return is worth something, but it only turns into silver when you use or sell what came back. The
calculators split the result in two:
silver in minus silver out for this run, not counting returned materials.
what the returned materials are worth at your prices.
Outpost's reference case: a craft sells for 3,000, its materials cost 2,000, they return at 20%, the station charges 100, and tax plus setup come to 10% of the sale.

Look at upfront silver to check you can afford the run, and at cash profit if you'll sell the returns cheap or not at all. Total profit is only right if you reuse or sell the returned materials at the prices you entered.

You pick which materials count toward returns. Artifacts, faction tokens, enchanting runes, souls and relics, and Dragon Blood never return, so the tools leave them out no matter what you tick. Player-run stations charge a fee per craft, which goes in
. Fixed silver costs that are part of a recipe get their own line as

covers how the rate gets set.
Your typed prices stay marked as yours

The production and transport tools load market prices where there are any, each with the city and time it was seen. If you type your own price, the tool marks it as yours and keeps it separate from loaded prices, and refreshing the market won't overwrite it. If an ingredient or output has no price at all, the result stays unavailable rather than counting the gap as zero.

The buy and sell methods chosen, so the right fees apply.

Dragonfire removed it from every weapon as a seasonal test, to push ZvZ away from plate melee DPS. Melee-heavy ZvZ comps lost their main answer to tanky frontlines, so expect more ranged and caster DPS in big fights.

Dragonfire cut the most damage reduction a group can stack on a mob from 80% to 50%, and the health reduction from 50% to 25%. Two debuff supports in a PvE comp overlap more than they used to, and one support plus extra damage is often better.
No IP cap and no PvP, so bring your best PvE gear. The mobs are immune to forced movement, so knockbacks and pulls don't do much there.
